newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland likely to help world force in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Ireland likely to help world force in Zaire.

text.p: Ireland is likely to contribute a small number of troops -- fewer than 100 -- to a multinational force being assembled to protect aid routes in Zaire, officials said on Thursday.
They said Irish involvement was likely to be limited to logistical and technical support but its participation was expected to be agreed in coming weeks.
The involvement of Ireland, which is a neutral state, would have to be approved by parliament but that was expected to be a formality with only a few dissenting voices.
They said it would be part of the European Union's contribution towards the force, which is to be led by Canada with support from the United States and other EU countries.
The force is being assembled under the United Nations umbrella and its provisions for peace enforcement which are compatible with Irish neutrality.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, whose country holds the current EU presidency, was an enthusiastic supporter of Dublin's involvement, the officials said.
Irish involvement was likely to be limited to less than 100 soldiers providing either transport or communications support for the force.
Around 80 Irish soldiers were involved in a similar United Nations effort in Somalia in the early 1990s when they helped keep aid routes open in the Northwest famine area of Baidoa.
EU involvement in the world army being assembled for Zaire will be discussed by EU officials at a meeting in Brussels on November 25, the officials said.
That meeting is expected to endorse EU involvement in the force, support for which is growing in EU capitals, the officials said.
"This is developing a momentum throughout Europe. The Tanaiste (Foreign Minister) is very keen to see Irish involvement," one official said.
Washington's readiness to provide an airlift for the force was crucial, they said.

The size, scope and role of the force is expected to become clearer after Canada, which will take the lead in the operation, writes to the U.N. Security Council on Thursday outlining its concept for the force, the officials said.
Ireland has scores of aid workers across Africa, many of them in the front line of the operation to find and feed hundreds of thousands of displaced Rwandan Hutu refugees.
